title: Clean Monday
hookLine: the Orthodox begin Lent on a Monday with kites, simple food, and forgiveness asked of everyone

cards: "Forgive me." The words go down a line of people in an Orthodox church on a Sunday evening. The priest bows to the first person in the congregation and asks it.
Then that person turns to the next. Old women ask teenagers. Husbands ask wives.
Someone asks the neighbor they haven't spoken to since the autumn. By the end, the line has reached everyone.

The next morning, in Greece, families drive out to the hills with bread, olives and vegetables, no meat, no cheese, and fly kites against the sky. A day of forgiveness, then a day of wind and plain food.

teach.b: Yesterday was the Western way into Lent, with confession and pancakes before Ash Wednesday.
Orthodox churches keep their own calendar for the season, and their Lent opens differently: on a Monday, and not with ashes but with a long chain of people asking pardon.

The Sunday before is Forgiveness Sunday. Its Gospel includes Jesus's words from the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you."
So the church takes it literally. Before the fast starts, everyone asks forgiveness of everyone, whether or not they think they did anything wrong. It isn't a trial.
Nobody has to prove who started it. The point is to go into the season with nothing owed. Then comes Monday, called clean in two ways.
Clean in the kitchen: the meat and dairy are gone, and the food turns simple. And clean in the heart, which is why the forgiveness came first.
The prophet Isaiah has a line that could hang over the whole day: "Wash you, make you clean."
And the kites? Nobody in the Bible flies one. In Greece they're simply part of how families keep the day, outdoors, together, looking up.
Some readers like the picture: a season that begins with eyes lifted and the weight a little lighter, on a hillside with the people you just asked to forgive you.

how: Orthodox Christians attend Forgiveness Vespers on the Sunday evening before Lent, where each person asks forgiveness of the others; on Clean Monday they begin the Lenten fast from meat and dairy, and in Greece families often picnic outdoors and fly kites.

games.q: it's Forgiveness Sunday evening. the line reaches you, and the next person is the one who hurt you, not the other way round. what do you do?
o: skip them; they owe you the apology.
bow and say forgive me anyway.
games.why: the custom is that everyone asks forgiveness of everyone, regardless of who was at fault. nobody has to prove who started it.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'd ask to forgive you: a sibling, a coworker, a friend gone quiet. In the Orthodox custom you ask even when you're not sure what you did.
Picture their face and say the two words to them in your mind, forgive me, and if you pray, bring them before God; if not, just hold them kindly.
